what: Matson runs ocean shipping. Its core business carries containers and goods between the US mainland and Hawaii, Alaska and Guam, where it is one of very few carriers. It also runs an expedited service from China to Long Beach that delivers far faster than normal ocean freight, and a logistics arm arranging freight for others.
customers: Retailers, grocers, manufacturers and households shipping goods to the island and Alaskan markets, plus e-commerce and apparel companies paying a premium for fast China-to-US delivery.
money: Container and roll-on services to Hawaii, Alaska and Guam, plus the expedited China services.
Freight brokerage, warehousing and supply chain services.
moat: The domestic routes are protected by the Jones Act, which requires cargo between US ports to travel on US-built, US-crewed ships. Building such a ship is extraordinarily expensive, so the number of competitors on the Hawaii and Alaska routes is tiny and effectively fixed. The China expedited service is different: it is a premium product built on dedicated berths and fast turnaround, and customers pay for speed rather than price.
risks: The China expedited service earns enormous margins when shipping is tight and ordinary ones when it is not. Revenue fell from $4.3B in 2022 to $3.1B in 2023 as that premium evaporated.
Free cash flow of $153.0M is well below net income of $538.5M because the company is building new ships, which is a very large capital commitment.
Hawaii and Alaska economies are small and slow-growing, so the protected routes provide stability rather than growth.
Changes to the Jones Act, occasionally debated in Congress, would remove the protection that underpins the domestic business.
Only four analysts cover the stock, so the $292.50 average target rests on minimal coverage.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 11.5 times earnings and 8.3 times EV/EBITDA, modest for a business with legally protected routes.
Debt of $736.5M is small relative to the fleet’s value, and the balance sheet is conservative by shipping standards.
The Jones Act routes generate steady cash regardless of global shipping rates, which is unusual in an industry defined by volatility.
The expedited China service has structural demand from e-commerce companies who need speed, not just the spot-rate spike.
New, more efficient vessels lower operating cost per container for decades once the building programme is complete.
watch: The China expedited service’s rates and volumes. The domestic routes are predictable; this is the line that swings the earnings, and it is where the whole valuation debate sits.
view: Matson is two businesses in one hull and they could hardly be less alike. The first is a legally protected utility: the Jones Act requires cargo moving between US ports to travel on US-built, US-crewed ships, and building such a ship costs a fortune, so the number of carriers serving Hawaii, Alaska and Guam is tiny and will stay tiny. Those islands need everything shipped in. That revenue is about as predictable as shipping gets.

The second is the China expedited service, and it is the reason this stock moves. Matson guarantees fast delivery from China to Long Beach — dedicated berths, priority unloading, days instead of weeks — and charges a large premium for it. When global shipping is tight, that premium is enormous and the earnings look spectacular. When it is not, the service earns a sensible but ordinary margin. Revenue falling from $4.3 billion to $3.1 billion between 2022 and 2023 is that mechanism working exactly as designed, and anyone extrapolating a peak year here will be badly wrong.

What I think is genuinely underappreciated is that the expedited service is not purely a spot-rate play. E-commerce and fast-fashion businesses have a structural need for speed that did not exist a decade ago, and they will pay for it in normal markets too. That puts a floor under the premium that most people modelling this as a shipping cycle miss. It is why I would not value Matson as a pure cyclical.

At 11.5 times earnings and 8.3 times EV/EBITDA with modest debt, the price is reasonable for a protected franchise with a volatile growth engine attached. The thing to understand before buying is the free cash flow: $153 million against $539 million of net income, because the company is building new ships. That is a good use of money for a business whose ships last decades, but it means the cash yield is poor until the programme finishes. Four analysts and a $292.50 average is thin coverage for a $6 billion company — which is itself mildly interesting, because under-followed protected franchises are where mispricings live.
bull: E-commerce keeps a structural floor under the expedited premium while the protected island routes generate steady cash, and new ships cut unit costs for decades.
bear: The China premium normalises completely, the island economies grow slowly, and the newbuild programme consumes cash through a period of ordinary earnings.
